s: B. Privileges and Immunities Clause (Article IV).
"The Citizens of each State shall be entitled to all Privileges and Immunities of Citizens in the several States."
The clause bars a state from discriminating against citizens of other states with respect to "fundamental" privileges, those "bearing upon the vitality of the Nation as a single entity."
These include pursuing a livelihood, owning property, and access to courts, but not recreational hunting licenses (Baldwin v. Montana Fish & Game, 1978).
Does the law discriminate against out-of-state citizens (by residency)?
Does it burden a fundamental privilege (commercial livelihood, property, medical care, access to courts)?

If so, the state must show a substantial reason for the difference, and that the discrimination bears a substantial relationship to it (Supreme Court of New Hampshire v. Piper, 1985; United Building & Construction Trades, 1984).
Corporations and aliens cannot invoke the clause.
Unlike the dormant Commerce Clause, this clause has no market-participant exception, and Congress cannot waive it.
It is distinct from the Fourteenth Amendment's Privileges or Immunities Clause, which protects rights of national citizenship (see Part VIII).
